items.title: The screens you actually launch from
items.description: The screen you see when you launch Claude Code, Codex or Cursor Agent was built out of raw white-on-black utilities rather than the product's own palette — fourteen different text opacities, flat translucent fills, and a one-pixel grey outline around every box. That combination is what reads as black and white and grey lines: a flat rectangle, a hard edge, grey text, no depth anywhere and nothing for the eye to land on. The runtime picker, its setup panel and the external agent transcript are now built from the same token ramp as the rest of Vector. Depth comes from a vertical gradient on a real surface rather than from an outline; there are three text tones instead of fourteen; and the selected runtime is the single accent on the screen, glowing from within rather than gaining a bright border, because a bright border on a dark panel is exactly the look the design system warns against. Status dots carry a coloured halo as well as a hue, so ready, signed out and not installed stay distinguishable at six pixels. Your turn and the agent's turn no longer look like two identical grey boxes: one sits right and lifts, the other sits left and recedes. Code Archaeology got the same pass and one addition — the checkpoints are threaded on a single vertical rail, so a stack of near-identical rows reads as a history you can follow from the first checkpoint to the latest. It had also been painting itself a near-black that appears nowhere else in the product and using a purple one digit off the brand colour; both now come from the tokens. Project rules are genuinely per-repository. The panel asked the backend for rules without naming a repository, so every project's rules panel listed every project's rules, and deleting one repopulated it with all of them again. It now asks for the repository it was opened for, re-reads when you switch projects, and still lists rules you have switched off — the prompt filter drops those, and reusing it here made a disabled rule impossible to find and turn back on. Project rules also left the task sidebar. It was a third door to a panel already reachable from the home screen when you pick a repository and from Settings, and the sidebar is for the task you are in. Finally, an updater that cannot run now says so. Automatic updates only work in a released build; a local build has no release channel to check, and the row rendered a greyed-out Check now button with no explanation, which reads as a broken feature rather than a build without a feed.

items.title: Tested from the outside
items.description: Version 1.19.96 is a reliability pass across the path from choosing a repository to shipping the result. Start a session in a different project and Code, Browser, Review, Terminal, Rules, MCP, plugins and the other project surfaces now follow the repository you actually selected; cloud release state remains scoped to that project across chats, and malformed route, event, session or workspace identifiers can no longer become a fake project or send an update to the wrong session. Automations refresh across repository changes and app focus, retain their last good state if a refresh fails and show the error. Rules and local memory also show load and save failures instead of silently looking empty, while manually edited rules and global rules survive synchronization. Vector now probes Claude Code, Codex and Cursor Agent for local sign-in state and stops presenting a runtime as ready when its CLI confirms it is signed out. Follow-up drafts stay with their own workspace, the first Codex response no longer claims the conversation restarted, and abandoned external runs have a bounded timeout and process-tree cleanup. The editor hides dependency and build folders and relies on the workspace language service for TypeScript and JavaScript diagnostics, removing duplicate isolated-file warnings. Trust boundaries received the same pass: browser typing re-checks the focused field before every character it sends, release secret scans fail closed when they cannot inspect the full tree, GitHub CLI discovery uses the user's login-shell path, and teammate messages use durable, idempotent delivery. The website now passes full Astro validation, distinguishes its fixture-driven interface preview from the desktop runtime, discloses that an existing local-memory file is automatically included in built-in agent context sent to the chosen model provider, hands protected card fields back to the user consistently, and keeps its navigation and product totals useful without JavaScript.

items.title: Straight lines
items.description: Work is gone. It was built last release and it is not what Vector is for, so it has been removed rather than left in the sidebar collecting dust. Four surfaces got the same treatment Automations got. Settings cards had their heading inset at 18px and their contents at 14px, so on every card in the app the title sat very slightly proud of everything beneath it; both are 18px now, the page header carries a rule so it reads as a header, and the Rules page stopped inventing its own form styling with inline styles and uses the shared fields like every other panel. The Agent Dashboard dropped the strip of seven counters above the board — three of them were Working, Needs you and Done, which are the column headings directly underneath, so it was the same number printed twice — keeping only what the columns cannot say, and its column headings now share one treatment with the rest of the app. The new workspace panel had three different sizes of uppercase section label in a single dialog, at three different opacities; there is one now. And the code editor's header was painted #101010, a near-black that appears nowhere else in the product and is darker than the canvas it sits on, which is why that screen never looked like the rest of Vector; it uses the sidebar token now. The help assistant also stops repeating the server's own words at you. It has been answering with an internal message about request protection, which describes a problem on our side and gives you nothing to do about it — it now says plainly that the outage is ours, and where to reach us.

items.title: Where the work comes from
items.description: Work is the new surface in the rail, and it is the piece that turns Vector from a coding tool into somewhere the job actually starts. It reads the tickets assigned to you — GitHub issues through your own gh sign-in with nothing to connect, plus Linear and Jira once you paste a token — and groups them the way you already think about them: in progress, in review, to do, done. Each tracker's own vocabulary is normalised on the way in, so Backlog and Icebox and To Do all land in one column and a board built from three systems still reads as one list. Pressing Start an agent hands the ticket over whole. Not the title retyped into a prompt — the description, the labels, the link, and the comments underneath, which is where the actual requirement usually hides. The agent is told to read the repository before changing anything and to say so plainly if the ticket is ambiguous or the code contradicts it, rather than guessing. What comes back is an ordinary isolated workspace on the same board, under the same review and merge flow as work started any other way. Every tracker is read independently, so one expired Jira token reports itself and leaves the rest of the board standing instead of quietly emptying it. Also fixed: the install command on the Pull Requests screen. Vector handed out one command per platform — brew install gh on a Mac, sudo apt install gh on Linux — and both fail often enough to matter. A Mac without Homebrew answers command not found, and gh is not in Debian's or Ubuntu's default repositories at all. Vector now looks for what is actually installed and only ever prints a command that can run; when nothing on the machine can install it in one step, it offers the download instead of a line that was always going to fail.

items.title: Levels, tickets, and where the money goes
items.description: The effort control was redrawn around what it actually is. Effort is four or five named levels, not a continuous quantity, so it is now one segment per level rather than a smooth bar — it reads as three of five at a glance, which a gradient never does, and it stops implying a precision the setting does not have. The lit run uses Vector's own gradient rather than a second palette, and at maximum a single highlight sweeps across it: one moving thing, not a field of them. The landing page gained two things. The first is what engineering work actually looks like: most coding tools stop at the code, but the work starts in a tracker and ends in a review, a deploy and a message to the people waiting. Vector reaches Jira, Linear, Slack, GitHub, Sentry and the rest of the catalogue through MCP, so a ticket is something an agent reads in full rather than something you paraphrase into a prompt — and the page now walks that round trip, from ticket to pull request to the channel your team is already watching. The second is an honest account of money. Licensing and model spend are separate and the page says so. Every purchase mints its own key; activation reads a stable machine identifier and immediately SHA-256 hashes it with a Vector-specific salt, so only the hash is ever sent and the raw identifier never leaves your computer; the activated licence is stored owner-only and replaced atomically; and if licensing cannot be reached Vector keeps working on the last good answer for seven days rather than failing closed on a timed-out request. Spend is measured from what the provider itself reported, an unmeasured run is recorded as unmeasured rather than as free, and the ledger stays on your machine.

items.title: The interface, in the page
items.description: The demo on the landing page did not look like Vector, and the reason turned out to be simple: it was drawn with the website's palette rather than the product's. The site is near-black with a vivid purple; the app is a grey ramp — #15141a canvas, #222028 sidebar, #201e27 surfaces, #35313f borders — with a muted #9274ec. It has been rebuilt from the app's own token file, so the frame, the sidebar, the panels, the type colours and the accent mirror values the product ships. The preview sidebar mirrors the app too: Project tools with Session, Agent Dashboard, Project rules, Code editor, Browser and Canvas, then Connections with Pull Requests, MCP and Plugins — the same labels, grouping, 32px rows and 7px corners. All nine sample surfaces go somewhere. There is a session view with a fixture transcript, tool calls and a composer; the composer is deliberately inert, because a prompt box on a page with no model behind it can only pretend, and it says so rather than swallowing what you type. The effort control was rebuilt to match its reference: a dark capsule, a blue-to-purple fill, a scattered starfield across it and a white circular thumb. The dots sit on three pitches with no common factor, so they read as scattered instead of as a grid, and at maximum effort the whole field drifts along the bar — each layer travelling a whole number of its own tiles, so the loop closes with no seam.

items.title: Room to breathe
items.description: The landing page stopped being a narrow ribbon down the middle of the screen. It had six unrelated container widths — 620, 820, 980, 1080, 1150 — which on any wide display left most of the screen empty while the content queued up in a column through the centre. There is now one measure for the whole page: 1240px for sections, 1440px for the app preview, and a hero that is wider without becoming harder to read. Feature sections became two columns wherever there is room, with the writing on one side and the interactive preview on the other, and each one alternating which side leads so the run of them stops reading as a single long column. The call to action moved inside the copy it belongs to, instead of orphaning onto a row of its own once the layout split in two. Below 1000px everything returns to a single column, and the line length in the copy stays around sixty characters at every width — wider was the goal, harder to read was not. Product screenshots were replaced with fixture-driven interface previews you can click: open a sample file, forget a sample memory fact, step through a browser check, pick a deploy target, or pause a sample automation before downloading the desktop app.

items.title: Three doors to your rules
items.description: Rules shipped in 1.19.7 and were almost impossible to find, which is the same as not shipping them. They now have three doors: Project rules in the workspace rail, a Set your rules card on the home screen next to Automations, and their own page in Settings. All three open the same panel, where you write a standard in plain English, point it at a repository and optionally at the files it governs, and Vector writes it to .vector/RULES.md in the repo for the whole team. Automations was redesigned. It had a close button floating alone above the title, four different text opacities competing inside one paragraph, and vertical spacing that changed with every block. It now opens under a real header bar that carries the title and the count, uses one spacing rhythm between sections, one uppercase treatment for every section heading and form label, and two text tones instead of five. The empty state reads as a state rather than a stray sentence, and the primary action is an actual primary button. The landing page demo grew from one screen into the app. A rail on the left moves between the Agent Dashboard, Codespace, your project rules and the browser, so you can look around Vector before downloading it — real clicks, real filtering, no video and no screenshots. The documentation gained four sections for everything added recently: Project rules, the Agent Dashboard board and its filters, running Claude Code, Codex and Cursor including how follow-up turns resume their conversation, and Automations.

items.title: Click around before you download
items.description: The Agent Dashboard's board grew up. Status, Team, Pull request and Agent are now labelled dropdowns rather than a loose row of chips — with four facets a bare chip loses its heading, and “merged” on its own never says which question it is answering. Each menu checks off the values you pick, the button carries what you chose, and the board narrows as you go: two values in one menu means either, values in two menus means both. Pull request now separates open from merged from never-opened, because a merged run still carries a pull request URL and would otherwise sit under “open” forever. The list view was rebuilt as grouped rows under the same three headings instead of a second, differently-shaped rendering of the same records, and both the board and the list now name the team a run belongs to above its task. And the landing page stopped being a gallery of screenshots. The Agent Dashboard now runs inside the page: switch the board to a list, open the filters, pick a status or a team or a pull request state, search across tasks, watch the columns recount and empty. It is real interaction against local data, not a video and not a picture, so you can decide whether you like Vector before you download anything. Every card in it is rendered with the page rather than assembled by script, which is why it still reads correctly with JavaScript yet to run.

items.title: Your house, your rules
items.description: Two things your team already does in review, now done by every agent. Rules are standards written the way you would say them to a new teammate — we don't put database query logic in the controller — pointed at a repository and, when it matters, at the files they govern. Vector saves them to .vector/RULES.md inside the repository itself, which makes them a committed, reviewable file rather than a preference buried on one machine: clone the repo and the rules come with it. Vector's own agents read that file on every prompt. Claude Code, Codex and Cursor read their own instruction files and would never see it, so Vector carries the matching rules into the prompt it hands them instead — one rule, written once, enforced by whichever agent picks up the work. A rule can be scoped to a folder or a glob, and the scope travels as words rather than as a pattern nothing downstream re-reads, so it still means something to the model. The Agent Dashboard now opens on a board: Running, Needs you, Done. Cards carry the task, what the agent is doing right now, how long it has been at it, and whether a pull request is already waiting. Search across names and tasks, then narrow by status, runtime, team, or to just the runs that opened a PR — two statuses means either, a status and a runtime means both, and the chips are built from the agents actually on screen so one can never empty the board. Needs you deliberately merges failed with needs review, including a finished run that reported an error: both are stopped and waiting on a person, and splitting them would put the same decision in two places. Teams stay first-class and filter as a unit, because in Vector they are not independent runs that happen to sit next to each other — they message each other while they work. Two connectors join the catalogue. Greptile connects through its own hosted MCP endpoint with your API key. CodeRabbit publishes no MCP server at all — it is an MCP client that reads other servers for review context — so the entry is the community server that reads CodeRabbit's review threads back off a GitHub pull request, labelled as community and authenticating with a GitHub token rather than pretending to be official. The catalogue count on the site was also four behind reality and now reads 118, which is what is actually there.

items.title: Agents you can talk back to
items.description: Launching a Claude Code, Codex or Cursor agent gave you a review page and nothing else. That was not a bug in the screen — it was the shape of the whole feature. Vector ran those CLIs in their one-shot batch modes, which accept exactly one prompt, run to completion and exit, so once a run finished there was nothing left to talk to. Worse, the conversation was thrown away: both CLIs announce a conversation id on their very first line of output, and Vector captured neither, so a thread that still existed on disk was orphaned the moment the run ended. External agents are now conversations. Vector records the agent's own conversation id as it appears, and a follow-up message resumes that same thread instead of starting over — the agent still remembers the file it just changed and why. The workspace drawer is now a transcript with a message box: your turns, the agent's replies, its live output while it works, and a quiet note whenever Vector itself steps in to repair a failed check. A follow-up that only asks a question no longer drags the whole check suite behind it. Two things had to be right for this to be honest rather than merely present. The id is captured on the line it arrives on, because the output buffer keeps only the most recent lines and Codex announces its thread exactly once, at the very top — read it any later and every real run would have lost it. And when a CLI refuses to resume, Vector re-briefs it with a written summary of the work so far and labels that turn as restarted rather than pretending the agent remembers. The runtime picker also stopped over-promising. It knew only whether a CLI was installed, so a signed-out Claude Code showed a green tile with its version number and then failed at the sign-in wall on every run — which is what made launching one feel broken. Vector now asks each CLI whether it is actually signed in, shows Signed out where that is true, and offers the one command that fixes it instead of telling you to reinstall something you already have. When a run does fail, the reason survives: the sentence naming the cause used to be discarded in favour of a dozen lines of raw machine output. Also fixed: discarding a workspace while its agent was still running made the failure handler itself fail.

items.title: Agents that actually reach each other
items.description: Putting agents in one workspace so they can message each other is something only Vector offers, and it did not work. The machinery was right — an agent really did queue its message — but there was one point where messages were read and one where they were written, and they sat at opposite ends of a run. Every member of a team starts at the same moment, so when the first prompts went out nobody had written anything yet, and by the time anything was collected everyone had already finished. The tool told each agent its message would arrive at the start of its teammate's next turn, and there was no next turn. Messages are now delivered while the team is still working, so one agent renaming a module can tell another to fix its imports and have that actually land. A repair pass counts as a turn and delivers too, and a run that fails or is stopped no longer strands whatever it had queued. Claude Code, Codex and Cursor agents can now be told what their teammates did, but they cannot reply — none of them has a teammate-message tool to call — so the launch screen now says which runtimes can send instead of promising it to all of them.

items.title: The boundaries hold
items.description: A symlink committed inside a project defeated the permission gate that keeps an agent within your workspace. The check compared paths as text, so a link placed by a dependency, a merged pull request, or an agent following instructions in a page it fetched gave read and write access to the rest of the disk with no prompt. Containment is now decided on where a path really lands, dangling links are followed by hand, and a file that does not exist yet is resolved through its parent, so creating one cannot escape either; a permission you already granted on a link keeps working, because only the containment decision changed. The edit tool could replace more than it was asked to and report success: a difference of a single space matched a whole indented line and wrote back an unindented replacement, and an anchored match swallowed a line the model never saw. Edits are now reconciled against exactly what was described, and an edit that cannot be reconciled is refused rather than quietly applied. The browser's refusal to type into password, one-time-code and card fields was reachable only through one input path, so the agent's own key-press command walked around it; every path that can put characters into a field now shares the same check, decides on the focused element rather than a named selector, recognises a masked field whose type claims otherwise, and refuses on an unfamiliar key. Beyond those: the shell tool now tells the model when a command exits non-zero instead of leaving it to assume success, searching a single file no longer searches its whole directory, the Cloud Console and the agent's own cloud tool finally read the same saved setup, the secret scan inspects the directory that actually gets deployed, deployments are no longer silently cut off at two hundred files, publish and cloud logs are redacted, the file holding cloud environment variables is no longer world-readable, and joining an existing team no longer erases the pairing you configured.

items.title: Trust before autonomy
items.description: Vector now treats agent autonomy as a security boundary. Packaged builds seal the credential-vault key with the operating system's secure storage and stop visibly if no protected store is available instead of falling back to a plaintext vault. Agent shell confinement remains an opt-in preview on supported macOS and Linux hosts instead of being enabled during this release; set OPENCODE_SHELL_SANDBOX=1 to try it. When enabled, unavailable confinement needs explicit approval and linked-worktree Git objects, refs, and reflogs stay read-only, while web access and reads of common SSH, cloud, Kubernetes, Docker, environment, and private-key files ask first. The hosted help and bug-report endpoints now validate origins, content types, sizes, and structured fields, and use atomic Redis rate limits that fail closed in production before model or email capacity can be spent. First launch no longer forces the exhaustive tour. It presents a short activation path with a read-only starter task, keeps the full guide optional, and only marks provider setup and the first task complete after a real model response finishes successfully. V2 sessions now calculate model spend from catalog input, output, reasoning, cache read, cache write, and context-tier prices, honor authoritative Copilot billing metadata, persist normalized token breakdowns, and keep session totals exact through event replay, replacement, and revert paths; usage without a finite catalog price keeps the existing $0 compatibility fallback. Releases are now blocked on package typechecks, unit tests, and desktop and website build smoke tests; macOS artifacts must be signed and notarized, Windows installers must carry a valid signature and an updater publisher identity, every expected architecture is checked, checksums are published, and update feeds must succeed before the GitHub release becomes public. The objective agent eval expands from five tasks to eight with billing-idempotency, path-containment, and concurrent-allowance cases, plus repeated trials for exposing run-to-run variance. Embedded SDK hosts now resolve their database location when their runtime is built rather than capturing a stale import-time path. The subagents Vector delegates to are now named and described for the work they do — Explore, General, Judge, Debug, Migration, Performance, Review, Security and Test — each with its own mark, a summary of what it handles, and a read-only badge where that matches its permissions. They appear by name in the session timeline, in the Agent Dashboard, and on a new Subagents page in Settings. Settings also gains Voice and Personalization, where custom instructions you write are saved to the instruction file every new session already loads. The settings panels scroll again: they were scrollable all along, but the scrollbar was hidden, so a page taller than the dialog simply looked cut off.

items.title: Undo that keeps your files
items.description: Undo could delete the work it was meant to restore. Reverting a step that touched two or more files asked git which of them were in the snapshot without disabling path quoting, so any name that is not plain ASCII came back quoted, failed to match, and the file was deleted as though it had never been in the snapshot — including untracked work that existed nowhere else. That path was also the only one that never checked the snapshot was readable first, so an unreadable snapshot read as an empty one. Reverting a rename was worse: git collapses a rename into a single entry naming only the destination, so undo deleted the new file and never restored the original. Both are fixed, the batch now refuses to delete when it cannot read the snapshot, and each has a regression test that fails without the fix. Scheduled automations could never report success — the poller looked for a message shape the route it calls does not return, so every run polled to its six-hour ceiling and was recorded as failed. A parallel agent whose turn ended in a provider error was recorded as complete with no changes, on exactly the unattended path the feature exists to protect. Merging was impossible in any project with local dev dependencies, because an isolated workspace has no node_modules and the resulting exit 127 was treated as a failed check rather than a skipped one. Non-ASCII paths broke merges after they had already written to the project, and files with Windows line endings could never be merged hunk by hunk. The one function guarding a merge against data loss silently skipped symlinks and swallowed every copy failure. Vector's subagents now have names and faces: Scout the fox explores, Veri the owl judges, Rook the raven watches the boundaries, and six more, each shown by name in the timeline and in the Agent Dashboard, with a new Pets page in Settings introducing the whole crew. Settings also gains Voice and Personalization, where custom instructions you write are applied to every new session in every repository. Pull Requests moved to Connections and now lists your CI runs, turning a failed one into a repair prompt. Scheduled runs left the session sidebar, since Automations on the home screen replaced it. Adds Graphify to the plugin catalogue.

items.title: One workspace, evenly told
items.description: The site led with running many agents at once, which is one capability rather than the reason to use Vector. It now gives equal weight to nine parts of the same workspace — the editor with search, diagnostics and a terminal; local memory that stays on your machine; spend measured from what the provider actually reported; the browser that will not type into a password field; optional judge verification; deployments on accounts that are already yours; the connector catalogue; parallel agents; and recurring automations — with a section that states plainly where each one is conditional. The model effort control is now a rounded rectangle rather than a capsule, so its frame matches the handle inside it, and at full effort the dot matrix carries purple flowing toward the handle instead of a flat pulse. Repaired the first-run test, which had asserted onboarding copy that stopped existing when the tour was rebuilt on 10 August and had been failing unnoticed ever since.

items.title: Work that repeats, and agents you can pair
items.description: Scheduled work moved out of the session and onto the home screen as Automations, and became a real automation engine rather than a reminder. Write the task yourself, then choose the repositories it runs in and, for each one, a fresh session or an existing thread to keep adding to. Every repository reports its own result, so one failing does not condemn the rest, and a recurring task now computes its next occurrence from the rule itself instead of drifting forward from whenever the last run happened to finish. A schedule missed while Vector was closed catches up once and says so rather than firing a burst. Agents can now be paired deliberately: a team is everyone-to-everyone, a coordinator broadcasting down to workers who do not chatter among themselves, or any pairing you set, and a message to an unlinked teammate is refused and told so instead of vanishing. Launching Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor Agent works again on ordinary machines: Vector looked for those CLIs using the stripped-down environment a desktop app inherits when it is opened from Finder, so anyone whose tools live under nvm, fnm, mise, asdf, volta, or a custom prefix was told the runtime was not installed, and the picker then hid it entirely. Vector now reads your login shell the way the engine already did, reports a runtime that is present but signed out as signed out with the command that fixes it, and shows an uninstalled runtime with its install steps rather than hiding the option. Fixed a defect that had been quietly deleting your work since 14 August: identifiers pack a millisecond timestamp into six bytes, which overflows and repeats roughly every 795 days, and the most recent repeat inverted the comparison behind tool-output retention — so every cleanup deleted the newest saved output and kept the oldest. Timestamps are now reconstructed across that boundary, with the identifier format unchanged. The test suite is green again: 24 failures, most of them assertions left behind by the rebrand, were repaired rather than deleted, and continuous integration, which had been running on a branch this repository does not have, now runs on every push.

items.title: Agents you can leave alone
items.description: Vector can now sandbox the commands its agents run. Enable OPENCODE_SHELL_SANDBOX and every shell command from an agent is confined to the workspace it belongs to by the operating system's own mechanism — a seatbelt profile on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux — with reads of SSH keys, cloud credentials, and keychains denied outright. Windows has no equivalent that ships with the OS, so Vector says so and runs unconfined rather than pretending. It is off by default and degrades to an ordinary command whenever a host cannot sandbox, so it can never cost you a command that used to work. Scheduled work now actually happens while you are away: Vector keeps a tray presence and stays resident after the last window closes, showing what is armed and when it next runs, notifying you when a run finishes, and never staying alive without a tray to quit from. Repository context stopped being a keyword search. An on-device structural index ranks files with BM25 over identifiers and paths, then spreads through the real import graph and the files git history shows change together, so an agent receives the code that matters instead of whatever happened to share a word with the request. Vector now remembers how a project fails: normalised failure signatures accumulate per repository, a repair that worked once is offered the next time the same failure appears, and a test that passes and fails without any relevant change is reported as flaky instead of being chased through another repair loop. Unattended spend is capped rather than merely displayed — five dollars a run and twenty-five a day by default for scheduled and background agents, with a run that reports no usage recorded as unmeasured rather than free, so it can never silently trip a limit. Adds an eval harness that scores Vector's own agent against objectively-checkable tasks, and can run the same set through the Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor runtimes for comparison. The model effort slider is now a dot matrix that brightens toward the level you pick. Fixed continuous integration: tests and typechecks were gated on a branch this repository does not have, so no push had run them.

items.title: Nothing spends your key without saying so
items.description: Vector silently rerouted prompts it judged complex to a stronger model — on a bring-your-own-key product that can be many times the token price you chose — while the composer kept showing the model you picked, so there was no way to tell what you were being billed for. Routing is now off by default, has its own setting, honours models you hid in Settings, and switches the composer to whatever it actually used. Theme, colour scheme, and language controls returned: they existed only in a legacy shell that a hardcoded flag made unreachable, so the shipped app had no way to change any of them. Billing stopped re-posting stale Stripe metadata, which let two webhooks arriving together drop the checkout session and permanently invalidate a licence key that had already been emailed. A dead or wiped computer is no longer a permanent lockout — moving a licence is self-service and simply bounded. The one-installer-per-licence rule became a rate limit, and a download is recorded once the bytes arrive rather than before they are sent. The what's-new feed is now generated at build time; it had never existed, so the release-notes dialog had never run.

items.title: Merges that keep a copy
items.description: Merging an agent workspace back into a project that is not a git repository could destroy work permanently. The copy-mode merge deleted and overwrote files in the real project directly, and the "checkpoint" it promised beforehand was only a map of file hashes — enough to detect a conflict, but incapable of restoring a single byte. Both copy merge paths now copy every file they are about to overwrite or delete into the checkpoint first, and a non-git checkpoint stores real file copies alongside a README explaining how to put them back. The same guarantee already covered git projects and now covers all four merge paths.

items.title: Undo that cannot delete your work
items.description: Session snapshots were written as bare git trees with nothing pointing at them, so the engine's own scheduled garbage collection removed them after a week. Reverting to a collected snapshot then read as "this file was never in the snapshot" and deleted the file from your working tree, while reporting that the undo had succeeded. Snapshots are now anchored behind a ref so collection cannot reach them, a revert that cannot read its snapshot refuses to delete anything and says why, and a restore that fails no longer claims to have worked. Scheduled tasks became usable: the screen had no way to create one, so the list was always empty. It now has a real form with one-off, daily, weekday, and weekly schedules, and the suggestions fill it in. Agent teams were running unisolated, because a coordination file was written into the workspace before the git worktree was created; git refuses to create a worktree in a directory that already has contents, so every team silently fell back to a plain copy. Teams now get real isolated worktrees. Files inside newly created directories were missing from every workspace diff. LLM-as-a-judge now applies to every prompt and every agent workspace instead of only the session you typed in, and a failed verdict must name the specific repair rather than only the problem. Model economics prices runs from the engine's own live rate catalog instead of a hand-maintained table that had no entry for the default models and billed cached tokens at ten times their real rate. An unsubstantiated performance comparison was removed from the site.

items.title: Agents can actually reach each other
items.description: Collaborative agents could not message each other. The teammate tool was registered in one tool registry while sessions resolve tools through another, so every call returned an unknown-tool error and the agent wrote its message into its own reply instead. The tool now lives where the engine looks, and the workspace is resolved through the location layer so the message queue lands in the right tree whether agents share one or work in isolation. Verified against a live model on a real repository: one agent renamed an export and told its teammate, and the teammate fixed the failing import.

items.title: Economics that actually learn
items.description: Model economics only ever learned from validated parallel runs, so it rarely gathered enough evidence to recommend anything. Every ordinary session now contributes what it truly cost — provider-reported tokens, spend, latency, and files touched — so recommendations appear from normal use. Removed a ranking signal nothing ever produced, which had been the primary sort key and rendered a permanently blank win rate. The site now says plainly which capabilities exist nowhere else: agents that message each other while working, per-agent attribution of live edits, and running Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor as engines inside Vector.

items.title: Licensing and disclosure
items.description: Removed the last copyleft dependency: HEIC images are now converted by the operating system rather than a bundled LGPL decoder, which also drops about three megabytes from every build. Expanded the privacy policy to cover local memory, the help assistant, bug reports, and optional screen and desktop control, and added a terms section describing what Vector can do on your machine and on services you connect.

items.title: Plugins that install themselves
items.description: Connecting a plugin no longer sends you to a terminal. Vector resolves whatever runner a plugin needs, fetches it when it is missing, and pins an interpreter the package can actually run on, so Computer Use — full desktop control with screen reading, mouse, keyboard, and window management — connects on machines that had neither uv nor a recent Python. Retired the in-session Review PR button in favour of Project tools, Pull Requests, which lists, reviews, and merges rather than acting on one pasted link.

items.title: Agents that work together
items.description: Agents can now share one workspace instead of each getting their own: they see each other's edits as they happen, message each other while working, and Vector names the file and both agents when two of them hold the same one. The Agent Dashboard in Project tools shows every agent live with its task, model, spend, and the conversation between them, and the code editor attributes each edit to the agent that made it. Adds Pull Requests with Vector AI review, local memory that follows you across every repository and can be erased outright, a Vector Help AI Assistant answering only from Vector's own documentation, one-click bug reporting, selectable Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor runtimes, and a rebuilt Scheduled tasks screen with real recurrence.

items.title: Real spend, real answers
items.description: The model economics engine now records the provider's own reported tokens and cost for every run instead of estimating from character counts, and ranks models on measured spend once correctness ties. Added the Vector Help AI Assistant, a docs-and-chat side panel answering strictly from Vector's own documentation so it cannot invent controls that do not exist. Replaced the workspace settings gear with a one-click bug reporter that sends your app version and platform along with the report.
